summary: On His last journey to Jerusalem, Jesus stops for a blind beggar the crowd wanted silenced, and gives him his sight.
key_insight: Moments earlier, Jesus asked James and John the very same question: “What do you want Me to do for you?” They asked for thrones. The blind man asked to see.
story: Jesus crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho, the last stop for pilgrims before the long climb to Jerusalem. Passover was a week away, and the road was crowded with people going up to the feast.

By the roadside sat a blind beggar, Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus. {Mk} With him, Matthew tells us, sat a second blind man. {Mt} Hearing a crowd going by, Bartimaeus asked what it meant, and they told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. {Lk}
He began to cry out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Many warned him to be quiet, but he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”

Jesus stood still and told them to call him. The same people who had hushed him now said, “Be of good cheer. Rise, He is calling you.” Throwing aside his garment, Bartimaeus rose and came to Jesus. {Mk}

Jesus asked, “What do you want Me to do for you?” He answered, “Rabboni, that I may receive my sight.” {Mk} Jesus had compassion and touched their eyes, {Mt} and said, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” {Mk}
Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus on the road, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God. {Lk}
differences: Matthew tells of two blind men; Mark and Luke tell of one, and Mark gives his name.
Matthew and Mark place the healing as Jesus went out of Jericho; Luke says it happened as He was coming near Jericho.
Only Mark records the crowd’s “Be of good cheer,” the cast-off garment and the word “Rabboni.”
Matthew alone says Jesus touched their eyes; Luke alone adds that all the people praised God.

fit.question: Was there one blind man or two? And did the healing happen as Jesus was leaving Jericho or as He was coming near it?

points.label: One or two
points.text: Mark and Luke focus on the man the early church knew by name. Matthew counts both. Saying a blind man was healed is not saying only one was. Matthew counts two in the same way among the Gergesenes (Matthew 8:28), where Mark and Luke tell of one.

points.label: Two Jerichos
points.text: In Jesus’ day there was the ancient city of Joshua’s time and, about a mile away, Herod’s new Jericho with its palaces and gardens. Jesus could be leaving one and drawing near the other.

points.label: Two moments
points.text: McGarvey suggests the man first heard about Jesus as He entered the city, then waited by the road out of town, where the healing took place.

fit.note: The text does not tell us which answer is right, but each one is reasonable, and none requires an error. Each writer tells the truth from where he stands.
fit.short: Mark and Luke name the man the church knew; Matthew counts both. There were two Jerichos, old and new.

scene.label: The last stop
scene.text: Jericho lies far below sea level near the Jordan. From here the road climbs more than 3,000 feet over about 17 miles to Jerusalem.

scene.label: Passover crowds
scene.text: Pilgrims from Galilee and Perea passed through Jericho on their way to the feast. For a beggar, there was no better seat on any road.

scene.label: The garment
scene.text: A poor man’s outer cloak was his coat by day and his blanket by night (Exodus 22:26–27). Throwing it aside was no small thing.

scene.label: “Son of David”
scene.text: This was a royal title for the promised Messiah. A blind man says out loud what the crowd has not yet said. Days later the crowds will shout of “the kingdom of our father David” (Mark 11:10).

witnesses.matthew: Counts two men and notes that Jesus had compassion and touched their eyes. In Matthew the King of David’s line shows mercy to the poor on His way to the throne.
witnesses.mark: Gives the name, the cast-off garment, the crowd’s “Be of good cheer” and “Rabboni.” It reads like an eyewitness memory, and Bartimaeus was likely known in the early church. Mark ends with him following Jesus “on the road,” the road to Jerusalem and the cross.
witnesses.luke: Sets the healing at the entrance to Jericho, just before Zacchaeus. Two outsiders in one town, a beggar and a rich tax collector, lead to Luke’s summary of the whole mission: “the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is a week from the cross, with a crowd around Him and Jerusalem ahead, and He stands still for one man the crowd wanted silenced.
seeing.living: Jesus asks him to say exactly what he wants. Mercy with Jesus is never vague. Bring Him the real need, not a polite one, and be ready to follow Him on the road once He answers.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus stopped and asked you today, “What do you want Me to do for you?”, what would you say? What garment might you need to leave behind to come to Him?

preaching.big_idea: The crowd said, “Be quiet.” Jesus said, “Call him.”
outline: A cry the crowd tried to silence (46–48)
A question that searches the heart (51)
preaching.watch_for: Mark frames his whole section on discipleship with two blind men healed (8:22–26 and 10:46–52). In between, the disciples cannot see what Jesus keeps telling them about the cross.
